supplement.holds: The main text explicitly refers to a full design description, questionnaires, validation/extension figures, objective activity/time measures, Lee bounds and employment/occupation controls (p. 3); control-group ChatGPT use and two-stage least squares estimates (p. 4); raw-ChatGPT grading comparisons (p. 5); and fixed-time-arm and editing analyses (p. 10, notes 26-27). The saved PDF provides no separate numerical effects for overall grade, writing quality, content quality, or originality. The fixed-time contrast and the separately named grades have no stated analysis unit in the saved PDF; whether the supplement supplies these specifications also remains unconfirmed (p. 4, Productivity; p. 10, note 26; pp. 12-13, Fig. 1 note).

paper_design_summary: The manuscript reports recruiting 453 college-educated professionals on Prolific for two occupation-specific writing tasks (p. 3). Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT registration, guidance, and optional use on the second task or to an Overleaf-signup control, with performance measured before and after the intervention. Blinded professionals from the same occupations scored the outputs for quality and originality (pp. 3-4).

studies.label: Online experiment with professionals: occupation-specific writing with ChatGPT versus Overleaf signup

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were assigned between groups to register for ChatGPT, receive guidance, and optionally use it on the second task, or to register for Overleaf without being told they could use it. All participants were assigned a pre-intervention and a post-intervention writing task. Bonus-payment schemes were cross-randomized. Structure is mixed because between-person treatment assignment is combined with repeated task measurements; this is not a randomized crossover of AI conditions (p. 3, Method; p. 12, Fig. 1 note).
assignment.quote: We randomly assigned 50% of participants to the treatment group and the remainder to the control group.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Method, treatment-assignment paragraph and final paragraph; p. 12, Fig. 1 note
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 11, Data and materials availability: AEA RCT Registry https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/trials/10882; DOI 10.1257/rct.10882-2.1

arms.name: Treatment (ChatGPT)
arms.description: After the first task, assigned to register for ChatGPT, receive guidance, and optionally use it on the second task (p. 3). Registration succeeded for 92% and 80% chose to use it on the second task (p. 4, Takeup of ChatGPT). The first task was pre-intervention; universal absence of prior or self-initiated AI use is not established.

arms.name: Control (Overleaf signup)
arms.description: Assigned to register for Overleaf to match signup time and hassle; not told they could use it, and less than 5% reported using it (p. 3). This was the no-assigned-AI condition, but about 10-20% of controls used ChatGPT on the tasks (p. 4, Takeup of ChatGPT).

participants.exclusions: The manuscript reports 453 recruited professionals (p. 3) and attrition of 6% in control and 11% in treatment (p. 3, Method), without an explicit flow giving exact numbers randomized, excluded, or analyzed in the post-treatment grade regressions. Table 1 occupation rows have N = 235 control and 218 treatment; the baseline Average Grade (Task 1) row has N = 233 control and 211 treatment (p. 18). These are descriptive/baseline counts, not explicitly labeled assignment or post-treatment analysis counts, so they are not copied into those fields. The linear and convex incentive groups cover 80% of respondents and supply Fig. 1; the fixed-time group covers 20% (p. 4, Productivity; p. 12, Fig. 1 note). No exact analysis N is calculated from rounded percentages.
participants.who: Experienced, college-educated professionals recruited on Prolific: marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, human resource professionals, and managers (p. 3, Method).
participants.quote: we recruited 453 experienced, college-educated professionals on the survey platform Prolific and assigned each to complete two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks
participants.locator: p. 3, Method; p. 18, Table 1; p. 19, Table 1 notes; pp. 12-13, Fig. 1 note

ai_tool.how_used: Participants could choose how to use ChatGPT on the second task after registration and guidance (p. 3). The experiment ran January 27 to February 21, 2023 (p. 3, Method). The authors report mostly lightly edited or unedited ChatGPT output: 33% of treated participants reported submitting the initial output unedited and 53% reported editing. Those reporting editing were active for 3.3 minutes on average after a large paste (p. 5, Human-Machine Interactions).

task.description: Two occupation-specific professional writing tasks, including press releases, short reports, analysis plans, and delicate emails, with pre-intervention and post-intervention outputs (p. 3). These open-ended written outputs were judged partly on originality (p. 4), so they fit the creativity codebook through that output score. The task category is creative_writing; the paper primarily studies productivity and does not provide an overall-creativity score.
task.duration: Designed as 20- to 30-minute assignments (p. 3, Method). The fixed-time incentive group, 20% of participants, was required to spend exactly 15 minutes on each task (p. 4, Productivity).

outcomes.name: Average evaluator grade on the post-treatment task
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded experienced professionals in the same occupations graded output on a 1-7 scale; three evaluators saw each output, with average within-essay cross-evaluator correlation 0.44 (p. 3, Method; p. 10, note 23). Evaluators were rewarded for agreement with other evaluators (p. 9, note 22). Fig. 1B uses participant-evaluator observations: regression of pre-to-post grade change on treatment, occupation-by-task-order, incentive-arm, and grader fixed effects, with SEs clustered by person; coefficients are rescaled by the pre-treatment outcome SD (p. 12, Fig. 1 note). Fig. 1D reports raw post-treatment participant-evaluator grade distributions (pp. 12-13). Supplementary robustness analyses include Lee bounds, employment/occupation controls, and two-stage least squares for imperfect compliance (pp. 3-4). The text distinguishes average evaluator grades from the separate overall grade and three sub-grades; the exact aggregation of these scores is not described in the saved manuscript. The rating unit and person-clustered standard errors are confirmed specifically for Fig. 1B, and the rating unit for Fig. 1D; all panels exclude the fixed-time incentive group (pp. 12-13). The fixed-time contrast has no stated observation unit or regression specification (p. 4; p. 10, note 26). The shared outcome-level unit is therefore null because a common unit across the retained contrasts is not established; the confirmed Fig. 1 rating unit is preserved here and in the main contrast.

contrasts.reported: Text: average evaluator grades increased by 0.45 standard deviations (p<0.001). The analysis sample/model behind this text value is not specified separately. Fig. 1B, restricted to the linear and convex incentive groups: Treatment Effect 0.41 SDs; 95% CI [0.23, 0.59], rescaled to pre-treatment outcome SDs. Fig. 1D raw second-task participant-evaluator grade means: Control 3.802; Treatment 4.53. Abstract: output quality rose by 18%. The text and figure values are retained as distinct printed results; neither is an originality-specific estimate. Analysis unit: rating is confirmed for Fig. 1B and Fig. 1D only; the text does not separately specify the model underlying 0.45 SD.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Productivity, first paragraph; p. 12, Fig. 1B, Fig. 1D, and note; p. 13, continuation of Fig. 1 note; p. 1, Abstract

contrasts.reported: Fixed-time incentive subgroup (20% of participants; exactly 15 minutes per task): treatment increased grades by 0.33 standard deviations, described as not statistically significant. Note 26 says the confidence interval includes zero and treatment/control groups differ in average pre-treatment grades; no numerical interval or p-value is printed. The point estimate is positive; no_clear_difference records the reported uncertainty, not an estimate of zero. The analysis unit and regression specification are not stated; do not apply the Fig. 1 rating unit to this contrast.

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met in S1. Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT registration, guidance, and optional use while producing the scored second-task writing versus Overleaf signup (p. 3, Method). The reported 453 recruited people, hundreds of baseline participants in Table 1, attrition of 6% in control and 11% in treatment, and main incentive groups covering 80% support at least 50 people analyzed in this study (pp. 3-4, 18-19; p. 12, Fig. 1 note). Exact randomized and analyzed counts are not explicitly reported and remain null; no exact count is derived from rounded percentages. Blinded occupation-matched professionals scored the submitted outputs, explicitly including originality, which meets the output-creativity criterion (p. 3, Method; p. 4, Productivity). Unconfirmed analysis units, missing separate grade estimates, and the text/figure effect discrepancy affect extraction, not these eligibility decisions. No cross-person content-diversity or scored unassisted post-AI outcome is reported.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT assignment raised average writing grades by 0.45 SD in the text (p<0.001; p. 4) and 0.41 SD in Fig. 1B (95% CI [0.23, 0.59]; p. 12), while originality was reported to increase without a separate numerical estimate (p. 4).
open_questions: What are the exact numbers randomized and analyzed, overall and by arm/outcome? The saved PDF gives recruited and descriptive/baseline counts, not an explicit participant flow or post-treatment grade-analysis N.

Does the unavailable supplement report the separate overall-grade, originality, writing-quality, and content-quality effects, their uncertainty, scoring details, analysis units, and analyzed Ns? Its exact contents cannot be verified from the saved PDF; Fig. 1B does not establish the units of these separate analyses.
Which sample/model produced the text's 0.45 SD grade effect, and why does it differ from Fig. 1B's 0.41 SD for the linear/convex incentive groups?

What observation unit, regression specification, and numerical uncertainty were used for the fixed-15-minute grade contrast? The saved PDF reports 0.33 SD and an interval including zero, but Fig. 1 excludes this subgroup and note 26 refers to the unavailable Supplementary Materials.
notes: Both raw forms parsed successfully. The entire markdown conversion was read, including references, notes, all figures, and Table 1; no supplement or appendix is included in the saved PDF. All recorded study numbers were checked against PDF text, with Table 1 additionally extracted using PyMuPDF find_tables. No effect sizes or sample counts were computed. Shared-count correction: both forms coded 453 as n_randomized and 218/235 as randomized arm counts; the paper labels 453 recruited and Table 1 descriptive, so those fields are null. The baseline task is pre-intervention, not established as universally AI-free. Assignment contrasts have attrition and imperfect compliance; they are not labeled complete-sample intention-to-treat. The paper's average evaluator grade is its primary output outcome; originality and the other separately named grades are secondary paper outcomes. These primary labels describe the paper, not a new Atlas pooled-estimate selection. Only with_ai is answered. Time taken, grade inequality, job satisfaction, self-efficacy, automation beliefs, and follow-up use do not constitute separate creativity/diversity outcomes. Grade inequality concerns scores, not similarity of content. The follow-ups at two weeks and two months measure reported use and beliefs, not scored unassisted outputs (p. 6). The additional opportunity to revise first-task output after task 2 was given to 30% of the treatment group, but no scored effect for that intervention is printed (p. 4). Treated ChatGPT users did not receive higher average grades than raw ChatGPT output given to evaluators, but no numerical comparison is printed; this comparison does not answer one of the three Atlas questions (p. 5). The earlier draft described in retrieval.json is not used to supply counts or estimates. Reconciliation groups repeated statements of the same factual difference; outcome order/IDs, naming, equivalent prose, and compatible locator variants do not count as differences. n_unresolved counts unresolved entries in differences. Unconfirmed shared counts are also disclosed in agreed_fields_checked and in the unresolved supplement/count item. Final review independently covered the complete markdown, including references, figure/table notes and the document end, and checked the relevant PDF pages and Table 1 with PyMuPDF. All five challenge problems were corrected as unsupported extensions of an analysis-unit specification. Because the form supplies one unit field for all contrasts of an outcome, S1-O1.unit is null while its descriptions preserve the confirmed Fig. 1 rating unit; the fixed-time unit remains unconfirmed. S1-O2 through S1-O5 also have null analysis units. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical reconciliation, including its earlier unit codings and unresolved items; the final object records the subsequent decisions. Direct urllib requests with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 to the OSF posted-materials API and then the Science article both failed with WinError 10013 (socket access forbidden); no supplement or journal-version content was obtained. All remaining open items concern extraction and do not change eligibility.

open_items.item: Exact people randomized, overall and by arm, and the timing/reasons for attrition (open_questions[0]; unresolved reconciliation difference on supplement contents and counts). An author-provided participant flow would settle assignment-stage counts. This does not change criterion 2: the existing sample and attrition evidence supports the 50-person analyzed threshold (pp. 3-4, 18-19).

Exact people analyzed, overall and by arm/outcome, including incentive subgroups (open_questions[0]; the counts portion of the unresolved supplement/count difference). Posted analysis data and code identifying the retained participants would settle these Ns. Criterion 2 is already supported above the threshold; counts remain null pending verification (pp. 3-4, 12-13, 18-19).

Whether the Supplementary Materials contain separate overall-grade, originality, writing-quality, and content-quality effects, uncertainty, rubrics, analysis units, and Ns (open_questions[1]; unresolved reconciliation difference on supplement contents; S1-O2 through S1-O5 challenges). Inspecting the supplement would establish its actual contents and any supplied specifications. Criterion 3 is already met by the explicitly output-scored originality grade (pp. 3-4); missing numerical/model details affect extraction.

Which sample/model produced the text value of 0.45 SD and why Fig. 1B prints 0.41 SD (open_questions[2]; unresolved reconciliation difference on the sample for 0.45 SD). An author explanation identifying the models or any reporting error would settle the discrepancy. Both printed results are retained separately; no eligibility criterion depends on their size or difference (p. 4; p. 12).

The fixed-15-minute contrast analysis unit, regression specification, and numerical uncertainty (open_questions[3]; S1-O1 challenge). The Supplementary Materials referenced by note 26 are needed to verify these details; the saved PDF excludes this subgroup from Fig. 1. No eligibility criterion depends on this robustness specification because the same study already qualifies (p. 4; p. 10, note 26; pp. 12-13).
